\chapter{Sorry}
\label{ch:hi-sorry}
\hlchaptermodality{9}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can apologise in Hindi with \hi{माफ़} \hi{कीजिए} and reach for its more formal cousin when the moment calls for it.}

Say \hi{माफ़} \hi{कीजिए} as 'please do forgiveness', then \hi{क्षमा} \hi{करें} when the setting is formal.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\hi{माफ़} \hi{कीजिए}]{\hi{माफ़} \hi{कीजिए} (māf kījiye) — please forgive me / sorry}

\label{lesson:HI-C09-maaf-kijiye}



\begin{quote}
You already know the formal \textbf{\hi{कृपया}} (\emph{kṛpayā}), \textquotedblleft{}please.\textquotedblright{} Hindi's everyday \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{} is built the same way you build a request: \textbf{name the kindness, ask for it to be done.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{माफ़}} (\emph{māf}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{forgiven, pardoned}\textquotedblright{} — not a native Hindi word at all! It's borrowed through \textbf{Persian} from \textbf{Arabic} \textbf{\ar{عفو}} (\emph{ʿafw}), \textquotedblleft{}to pardon, efface, wipe away {[}a wrong{]}.\textquotedblright{} Look closely at the spelling: the dot under \hi{फ} (called a \textbf{nuqtā}) turns the plain \emph{pha} sound into \textbf{fa} — Hindi's way of writing sounds that arrived from Persian and Arabic.
  \item \textbf{\hi{कीजिए}} (\emph{kījiye}) = the \textbf{respectful imperative} \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{please do},\textquotedblright{} from \textbf{\hi{करना}} (\emph{karnā}), \textquotedblleft{}to do.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

So \textbf{\hi{माफ़} \hi{कीजिए}} is literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{please do forgiven{[}-ness{]}}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{please make {[}this{]} forgiven.} It's the same light-verb move you've already met: naming a state (forgiveness, kindness, compassion) and asking someone to \emph{do} it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest about register — and about English creeping in}
\textbf{\hi{माफ़} \hi{कीजिए}} is warm and genuinely everyday — but Hindi keeps a \textbf{more formal, Sanskritic} cousin for writing and ceremony: \textbf{\hi{क्षमा} \hi{करें}} (\emph{kṣamā karēṁ}), \textquotedblleft{}please grant \textbf{kṣamā}\textquotedblright{} — from Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{क्षमा}} (\emph{kṣamā}), \textquotedblleft{}patience, forbearance, forgiveness.\textquotedblright{} Where \emph{kṛpayā} was the bookish \textquotedblleft{}please,\textquotedblright{} \textbf{kṣamā karēṁ} is the bookish \textquotedblleft{}sorry.\textquotedblright{}

And here's the honest twist: in casual conversation, many Hindi speakers simply say the \textbf{English word \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{}} outright — it has been fully adopted into everyday Hindi, the same way English \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} sometimes stands in for \emph{kṛpayā}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}māf\textquotedblright{} — forgiven — then \textquotedblleft{}kījiye,\textquotedblright{} please do
  \item the whole phrase — \textquotedblleft{}māf kījiye\textquotedblright{} = please forgive me
  \item the formal cousin — \textquotedblleft{}kṣamā karēṁ\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{माफ़} \hi{कीजिए}} literally mean? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Please do forgiven{[}-ness{]}\textquotedblright{}} — \emph{māf} \textquotedblleft{}forgiven\textquotedblright{} + \emph{kījiye} \textquotedblleft{}please do.\textquotedblright{}) Where does \emph{māf} come from? (\textbf{Borrowed via Persian from Arabic} \emph{ʿafw}, \textquotedblleft{}to pardon.\textquotedblright{}) What's the more formal, Sanskritic cousin? (\textbf{\hi{क्षमा} \hi{करें}} \emph{kṣamā karēṁ}, from \emph{kṣamā} \textquotedblleft{}patience/forgiveness.\textquotedblright{}) What do many Hindi speakers just say instead, casually? (\textbf{The English word \textquotedblleft{}sorry.\textquotedblright{}})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ā]{\hi{आ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:HI-S04-letter-aa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \hi{अ} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{आ}}
\textbf{\hi{आ}} — \emph{ā}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape the vowel \emph{ā} takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside a word.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the joined upper-and-lower left body of \hi{अ}
  \item a middle shoulder
  \item an inner vertical stem
  \item a trailing vertical stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \hi{आ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{आप} / \hi{तुम}} — you (respectful / familiar)
  \item \textbf{\hi{आपका} \hi{नाम} \hi{क्या} \hi{है}?} — what's your name?
  \item \textbf{\hi{आप} \hi{कैसे} \hi{हैं}?} — how are you? (respectful)
  \item \textbf{\hi{आपका} \hi{स्वागत} \hi{है}} — you're welcome (also \textquotedblleft{}welcome!\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{आ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} curve around the upper bowl, then continue down and around the lower bowl without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and sweep the middle shoulder right
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the inner stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the trailing stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{5.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 4.} The pen comes up 4 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified modern printed teaching form; other Devanagari traditions split the shared \hi{अ} body into more strokes.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari \hi{आ} stroke order.svg’, frames 1–5, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \hi{आ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{आप} / \hi{तुम}  ·  \hi{आपका} \hi{नाम} \hi{क्या} \hi{है}?  ·  \hi{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{आ} three times, saying \emph{ā} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \hi{आ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \hi{आ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ā}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pa]{\hi{प} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:HI-S113-letter-pa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \hi{◌े} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{प}}
\textbf{\hi{प}} — \emph{pa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{p}, it is \textbf{pa}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a left stem curving around the lower bowl to its upper-right junction
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \hi{प} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{आप} / \hi{तुम}} — you (respectful / familiar)
  \item \textbf{\hi{आपका} \hi{नाम} \hi{क्या} \hi{है}?} — what's your name?
  \item \textbf{\hi{पाँच}} \emph{pāṁch} — Sanskrit's nasal consonant survives inside the Hindi vowel
  \item \textbf{\hi{कृपया}} \emph{kṛpayā} — please (kṛpayā — \textquotedblleft{}kindly,\textquotedblright{} from kṛpā \textquotedblleft{}grace/compassion\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{प}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} descend the left stem, then curve right around the lower bowl and rise to its upper-right junction without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified three-stroke teaching form; everyday handwriting may join or simplify the bowl differently.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\hi{प}-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \hi{प} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{प} three times, saying \emph{pa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \hi{प} once more
\end{itemize}
